books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

stimulus.text: Margaret Fuller, a member of Emerson's circle in Concord, published Woman in the Nineteenth Century in 1845. She argued that women, like men, should be free to develop their minds and characters, and she edited the transcendentalist journal The Dial. The photograph shows Fuller in 1846, seated in profile, reading a book on a stand with her hand raised to her forehead.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the lesson script on transcendentalism: Emerson's circle included Margaret Fuller, whose 1845 Woman in the Nineteenth Century fed the Seneca Falls generation. Photograph: daguerreotype of Margaret Fuller by John Plumbe, Jr., 1846 (National Portrait Gallery). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Description records only what the photograph visibly shows.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Fuller's place in Emerson's circle best illustrates which feature of transcendentalism?

options.text: A small New England circle, not a mass movement
It drew its largest crowds in the South
options.misconception: Revivals drew crowds in the South, so it is easy to give transcendentalism the same map.

options.text: It was organized as a church with ordained ministers
options.misconception: Emerson had been a minister, so it is easy to think the movement was a church.

options.text: It taught that individuals should obey institutions
options.misconception: Movements usually have rules, so it is easy to assume this one taught obedience.

rationales.A: The stimulus names a circle in Concord: Emerson, Thoreau, Fuller, and a few friends, not a national crowd.
rationales.B: The circle was centered in Concord, Massachusetts; its writers were New Englanders, not Southern crowds.
rationales.C: Transcendentalists distrusted institutions, including churches; they were writers and thinkers, not a denomination.
rationales.D: Their core teaching was self-trust against institutions, the opposite of obedience to them.
rationales.general:
1. Count the circle. The stimulus names Emerson's circle in Concord — a roomful of writers, not a revival tent.
2. Ask what smallness means. A circle of friends can change how a few thinkers write, without becoming a mass movement.
Background from the books: transcendentalism was never a mass movement, but it fueled the reform era's ideas.
Remember: size matters — a circle and a crowd are different kinds of power.
